title: Trump Extends $100,000 H-1B Fee to September 2027 as New Order Ties Filings to Employer Layoffs
excerpt: Two September 18 actions reshape the H-1B program: the $100,000 payment policy is extended through September 2027, while a separate executive order directs federal agencies to weigh an employer's layoff history when adjudicating filings.
body:
• On September 18, 2026, President Trump signed two H-1B actions: a proclamation extending the $100,000 fee policy through September 21, 2027, and an executive order directing agencies to consider employer layoffs in H-1B decisions.
  • The fee targets new petitions for workers outside the United States who need consular processing; renewals, amendments, and change-of-status filings inside the US are exempt.
  • USCIS is not collecting the fee right now. A Massachusetts federal court vacated the policy on June 8, and the First Circuit refused on July 24 to pause that ruling while the government appeals.
  • If you already hold an H-1B visa or had a petition approved before September 21, 2026, the fee does not apply to you — and an extension-of-stay filing carries no $100,000 charge regardless of how the litigation ends.

The two September 18 actions

President Trump issued a pair of presidential actions on September 18 affecting the H-1B program, and they do very different things. The first, a Presidential Proclamation titled "Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers," extends for 12 months the $100,000 payment requirement first imposed by Proclamation 10973 in September 2025. The restriction now runs through September 21, 2027. The second, an Executive Order on "Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Program," directs the Departments of State, Labor, and Homeland Security to review H-1B filings more aggressively and to share information across agencies.

The proclamation continues to target a narrow category: H-1B petitions for beneficiaries who are outside the United States and must seek admission to effectuate the approval — including through consular notification, port-of-entry notification, or pre-flight inspection. It retains discretionary national-interest exceptions.

"A routine H-1B renewal filed today carries no $100,000 charge, and the court order means no one is paying it anywhere."

The fee nobody is paying

The extension arrives with a major legal caveat. On June 8, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the agency policy implementing the $100,000 fee, finding it functioned as an unauthorized tax imposed without congressional approval — a violation of the separation of powers and the Administrative Procedure Act. The government appealed, but on July 24 the First Circuit Court of Appeals denied its request to pause the ruling while the appeal proceeds. USCIS states on its website that it will comply with the court's order: the fee is not owed at this time.

Immigration counsel widely read the vacatur as covering the extension too, since it continues the same payment policy, though no court has yet ruled on the extension itself. The legal picture is split: a separate federal court has allowed the fee to stand in another case, and the administration's appeal remains pending. The extension signals intent to reinstate collection if the litigation resolves in its favor.

The layoff test

The executive order breaks newer ground. It directs the Secretaries of State, Labor, and Homeland Security to take into account, in any labor condition application, petition, visa, or entry decision, whether the sponsoring employer directly or indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous 12 months — or plans future layoffs that negatively affect the employment of similarly situated U.S. workers. It also directs the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division to begin reviewing data from previously submitted labor condition applications to determine whether enforcement action against sponsoring employers is warranted.

Unlike the fee proclamation, this order is not blocked by any court. Employers with recent or anticipated workforce reductions face a harder adjudication path starting now.

What it means for H-1B workers

For the Indian professionals who make up roughly seven in ten H-1B holders, the practical takeaway is more reassuring than the headlines. The $100,000 fee does not apply to petitions for beneficiaries who hold an H-1B visa or had an approved petition filed before September 21, 2026, and it does not apply to amendments, changes of status, or extensions of stay for workers already in the United States. A routine H-1B renewal filed today carries no $100,000 charge, and the court order means no one is paying it anywhere.

The layoff order is the one that bites in practice. Workers at companies that have cut staff in the past year should expect tougher scrutiny of new filings — and prospective hires should ask recruiters directly about the employer's recent layoff history before committing to a sponsored petition.

What to watch

Three things will determine where this goes: the appeal in the fee litigation, where a loss for the government would end the $100,000 policy entirely; how agencies translate the layoff directive into actual adjudication standards; and whether the Wage and Hour Division's retrospective review of old labor condition applications produces enforcement actions that put current H-1B holders' employers in the crosshairs.
